Zilo AI is featured on Launch91 in a new piece on India's AI talent shortage.

The article looks at why companies are finding it so hard to hire AI talent, and why more of them are turning to contract hiring to keep projects moving. 

Some key takeaways: 
- ManpowerGroup's 2026 survey of over 39,000 employers found 72% struggle to fill roles, and AI skills are now the hardest to find globally 
- In India, that number rises to 82% 
- According to Ceipal, 1 in 4 roles at India's GCCs is now contractual, up from 1 in 5 two years ago 
- Roughly half of open AI positions can't be filled from existing applicant pools 

This is the problem we work on every day. We place AI/ML engineers, generative AI engineers, data scientists and developers on contract, and we typically share qualified profiles within 24 to 48 hours of receiving a JD. Alongside hiring, our team of 1,600+ annotation and ASR professionals has delivered over 10 million labeled data points for clients across retail, BFSI and healthcare. 

Thanks to the Launch91 team for the feature. 

Read the full story: https://lnkd.in/dwE27_-f

One thing I've learned from two-sided markets: the problem is rarely either side on its own. It is that nothing connects them.
 
A boutique recruiting firm, one of the most respected in the US, closed $250,000 in contracts in under two months once both sides ran through the same system.
 
Before that, all of it was manual. Engineers came to them looking for roles. Companies came to them looking for talent. Matching the right candidate to the right company on every open role, reaching out, following up and tracking each conversation, twice over, with nothing joining the two processes. By the time anyone got a reply, that person had already moved on.
 
Here is how the system works.
 
1. Capture the candidate conversation
 
- Every candidate call is recorded by Fireflies.ai and Granola.
- Claude Code processes the transcript and extracts structured data straight into Google Sheets.
- No manual entry at any point.
 
2. Enrich and personalise the outbound
 
- From Sheets, Clay takes over.
- Apify, Sculptor and Juicebox scrape companies actively hiring for that role in that location.
- Clay AI finds the right decision maker and writes a personalised first line for every contact.
 
3. Send it as though it came from him
 
- Outreach goes out through EmailBison on email and through the client's own LinkedIn account.
- Every message reads like it came from him directly.
 
4. Run the same system in reverse
 
- When a company sends a job order, the flow flips.
- Clay sources engineers who match the role, outreach goes out, and replies get tracked exactly the same way.
 
5. Categorise and route every reply
 
- AI sorts every incoming reply.
- Positive ones hit Slack in real time and get logged straight into Loops, the client's CRM.
 
The recruiter only steps in when someone is ready to talk.
 
What that produced: $250k in contracts, 5 deals signed, and the first one closed inside two weeks.
 
Working both sides of a market normally means splitting time across two manual processes. The leverage here was not automating either side faster. It was building one system that could run both directions, so the same reply handling served each of them.

The conversation around data engineering in 2026 has shifted from "building pipelines" to "managing outcomes." The first two months alone delivered more capable AI models than the prior two years combined, and the implications for our workflows are not hype -- they are structural.

The 2026 State of Data Engineering Report, based on over 1,000 responses, confirms what I have observed firsthand: platform-owned infrastructure is the new default. The era of each team siloing its own ETL logic is ending. Instead, we are converging on event-driven pipelines that treat data as a stream of facts, not a batch of snapshots. This is not just about latency; it is about enabling real-time decisioning without rebuilding your entire stack every quarter.

What is less discussed is how AI assistants have lowered the bar of entry into data engineering. Tools like dbt Copilot and SQL-aware agents are no longer novelties -- they are how junior engineers onboard and how senior engineers prototype. The non-obvious takeaway: this does not eliminate the need for deep technical skill. It compresses the time between an idea and a production pipeline, which means the bottleneck is now architecture and governance, not code.

Data governance has also matured from a checkbox exercise into a competitive advantage. With regulations tightening and data contracts becoming standard practice, teams that treat governance as a first-class concern -- not an afterthought -- are shipping faster, not slower. The key is embedding policy into the pipeline, not bolting it on afterward.

I am actively looking for my next role where I can apply this perspective to real, scaling problems. If your team is building platform-owned infrastructure, migrating to event-driven architectures, or looking for someone who can navigate the intersection of AI tooling and data governance, I would welcome an honest conversation.

Agencies have a bad rep. For myriad reasons: lack of industry knowledge, domain expertise, and too many commitments at once. 

I have worked with good and bad freelancers. While posting a contractual job opening, our team prefers working with independent contractors than agencies.

This time, we made a conscious choice to work with an agency instead.

The big project: Redesigning our website for Equip - Helping You Hire Faster. The old website only spoke of assessments and now the product range has expanded to include ATS, CV Screening and AI Interviews.

Here's how we chose a design agency to work with: 

1. Interview multiple, in parallel: This is hiring 101 but it is easy to get enamoured with a pretty portfoilio and be fixated on hiring them only to find out later that they cannot meet expectations. (More on why below) 

2. Set expectations: We were specific from the get go that we are not an early stage product. We have over 1000 customers so our team is very opinionated on what converts and goes into the website. We told the agency that even if their team can deliver a typical website revamp project in 7 days, we wanted to work with a team that can patiently iterate and understand our requirements. This alignment was critical to the success of the project.
 
3. Speak with the designer before signing the contract: The portfolio attached to the application is the best of what the agency offers. In most cases, it belongs to the most senior designer or the founder. Multiple junior designers are assigned to the project after it starts and then you have to watch it collapse faster than a house of cards. 

Look at their past work and critically analyse if they can deliver what you need. If you’re a SaaS company and you spot good designs for SaaS that match your vision, that’s a good sign.

4. Ask for the (read-only) source files of projects:  Anyone can claim a nicely designed website as their own. Find any proof that it is their work and not someone else's.

Most brokerages think their back office is a cost that grows with revenue. It actually grows with headcount, and those are not the same thing.

Watch a growing brokerage and you see the same curve every time. Sign ten more agents, and within a quarter you are hiring another coordinator. Sign ten more, hire another. Revenue steps up, but so does payroll, almost one for one. The efficiency you expected from scale never quite arrives.

The reason is that coordination is done by people, and people do not batch. Every file has its own dates, its own parties, its own exception that shows up on a Friday afternoon. You cannot spread one coordinator across forty files the way you spread one CRM license. So volume and headcount rise together, and the back office stays a linear cost no matter how big you get.

The brokerages breaking that curve are not working their coordinators harder. They are adding a layer underneath the work. When an AI control plane that orchestrates your stack reads every contract, tracks every deadline, and coordinates your TMS, CRM, signature, and comms, one coordinator can carry far more files without more misses. The cost stops tracking headcount and starts tracking software.

That is the difference between a brokerage that adds people to grow and one that adds margin. The first hits a ceiling every time the ops lead burns out. The second keeps the same lean team through the next fifty agents.

Back-office headcount is not a law of physics. It is a symptom of coordinating by memory instead of by system.

The AI hiring lawsuit that should actually be keeping HR leaders up at night is not about bias.

It is about the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

Two job applicants sued Eightfold AI, claiming that its screening system qualifies as a consumer reporting agency under FCRA. The allegation: the platform scraped personal data from outside sources, generated candidate scores, and removed people from hiring pipelines before a human ever saw their applications. All without disclosure, dispute rights, or the accuracy standards FCRA requires.

Most HR teams never framed their AI vendor contracts around this question. They audited for bias. They checked for disparate impact. They did not ask whether their screening tool had quietly become a credit bureau.

That distinction matters enormously right now. If courts rule that AI hiring systems producing scores from external data meet the FCRA definition of consumer reporting, the compliance obligation does not land on the vendor. It lands on the employer.

The disclosure requirements alone would restructure how most companies currently use these tools.

What this case signals is that the legal risk in AI hiring is moving faster than the audit frameworks HR teams built to manage it.

Are you tracking the FCRA exposure in your AI hiring stack, or is your legal team still focused primarily on disparate impact?

AGENTIC AI DEBATE: MCP vs Function Calling — are we solving the same problem twice?
Before MCP became one of the hottest terms in AI, developers were already connecting LLMs to external systems using:
Function Calling → APIs → Tools → Databases → Enterprise Applications
Now Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduces a standardized approach for exposing tools, resources, and context to AI applications.
So here's the question:
👉 When do you actually NEED MCP instead of regular function/tool calling?
🔧 FUNCTION / TOOL CALLING
→ Application defines available tools
→ Direct integration with APIs and services
→ Straightforward for smaller applications
→ Tight control over execution logic
→ Fewer architectural components
→ Works well when integrations are known upfront
🔌 MCP
→ Standardized interface between AI applications and external capabilities
→ Tools and resources can be exposed consistently
→ Useful across multiple AI clients
→ Reduces custom integration patterns
→ Supports increasingly modular agent ecosystems
→ Can improve interoperability between AI systems and tools
But here's where architecture matters.
Imagine your AI agent needs access to:
📧 Email
📁 Documents
🗄️ Databases
🎫 ServiceNow
💬 Slack
☁️ Cloud services
📊 Analytics platforms
🔐 Internal enterprise APIs
Would you build eight custom tool integrations directly into the application?
Or expose capabilities through reusable MCP servers?
🔥 And an even bigger question:
Is MCP replacing APIs and function calling?
I don't think that's the most useful way to look at it.
An MCP tool may still ultimately call an API, database, SDK, or internal service underneath.
The architectural question is really:
Where should the integration contract live?
If you were designing a production Agentic AI platform, what would you choose?
🅰️ Function Calling + APIs
🅱️ MCP-first
🅲️ MCP + APIs + Function Calling together
🅳️ Depends on integration scale and reuse requirements
👨‍💻 AI Engineers & Architects: Are you actually running MCP servers in production?
🎯 Recruiters: How often is MCP appearing in your Agentic AI requirements now?
🤝 Prime Vendors & Implementation Partners: Are clients explicitly requesting MCP experience, or is it still mostly a preferred skill?
🏢 Hiring Managers: Would you rather hire someone who knows MCP—or someone who deeply understands tool architecture, APIs, security and orchestration?
👇 A, B, C or D — and WHY?

AI in Compliance: The Biggest Misunderstanding

Most compliance teams treat AI as a decision-maker, not an assistant. Let's be clear: AI does not replace people. The only narrow exception is personal safety — and even then humans set boundaries and own accountability. Every final compliance decision remains human.

Myths

1. "AI will replace compliance officers." AI automates work, not accountability. Regulators assess human decisions, not algorithms.
2. "AI is objective." LLMs drop 25%+ accuracy on legal tasks; legal AI hallucinates 17-33%. AI can fail confidently.
3. "One tool solves everything." Rules and tactics evolve. Static AI goes stale.

What AI SHOULD Do

· Process massive data to surface signals (comms, transactions, docs)
· Reduce false positives (e.g., AML false-positive time cut 50%)
· Support investigations: translate, classify, summarize
· Track regulatory change; filter noise for humans
· Assist audit prep: collect evidence, generate checklists, flag missing items

What NOT to Use AI For

· Final risk assessments (client risk, SAR decisions)
· Judging compliance culture (tone at top, whistleblower interviews)
· Final contract approval (45% of legal depts say no)
· Audit readiness — see below
· Any decision requiring accountability

Audit Readiness: Why AI Can't Own It
Audit readiness isn't tidy files. It's proving controls work and defending that conclusion.

AI can collect evidence, generate checklists, organize docs. But it cannot:

1. Judge sufficient/appropriate evidence (e.g., management bias in board minutes, control exceptions in practice).
2. Challenge its own output. AI is confident when wrong. PCAOB warns reliance on AI may erode professional skepticism. If a human just confirms "AI passed," the audit trail says "AI review: passed" — not "human made professional judgment." That fails regulatory scrutiny.
3. Own final accountability. Workpapers must show what AI did, inputs/outputs, and human review. "We are audit-ready" is a human conclusion.

AI helps you prepare. It cannot make you audit-ready.

Key US Compliance Sectors & Why

· Financial Services (SEC, FINRA, CFPB, FinCEN): high volume, strict deadlines — AI monitors, humans file SARs and rate risk.
· Healthcare (HIPAA, FDA): sensitive data, clinical/legal consequences — AI assists, humans decide.
· Data Privacy (FTC, CCPA/CPRA, ~20 state laws, FISMA/FedRAMP): fast-changing rules — AI tracks, humans interpret.
· Digital Assets (GENIUS Act 2027, SEC/CFTC): rules still forming — human judgment where no precedent.
· Employment (EEOC, anti-discrimination): bias in, bias out — AI screens, humans own hiring.

Core Principle
AI is an accelerator, not a decision-maker. Humans review what AI flags — not just confirm it ran. Audit trails must show human judgment, not "AI review: passed."

Use AI for tedious parts. Use judgment for important parts.

The first time I went to university, connecting to the internet sounded like two fax machines in the throes of a passionate encounter. The second time, it offered to write my dissertation.

I wasn't a good student first time round. Not really. Vodka Red Bulls were 60p, printing a journal article cost more than a night out, and I seriously considered liberating toilet roll from a local bar. An early experiment in quantitative easing.

A marketing career later, I left a director role to learn how to learn again, in AI, a subject that was alien to me. In many ways it still is. It learns faster than I do, which I suppose is the point.

I did it in Bradford: city of Hockney, the Brontës, Zayn Malik and the legendary Harry Corbett, Sooty to anyone of a similar vintage. Wherever I've travelled, I come back, and I believe in it enough to put my money where my mouth is.

Beyond the lectures, the code that wouldn't run and scanning the room for anyone who didn't refer to anything pre-noughties as vintage, it was quite a year. Trade wars, actual wars, dynamically priced Oasis tours, and Bradford hosting an international quantum hackathon. I only helped organise one of those. Guess wrong and I'll put a tariff on you.

I was humbled, embarrassed, and knocked on my backside more than once by academics and peers. My old confidant Epictetus, revived with smelling salts and a strong Yorkshire Tea, reminded me it's impossible to learn what you think you already know. That's bad news for a marketer with a decade of opinions. I had a hell of a lot of unlearning to do.

Fast forward 18 months and I left with a Distinction, and the look of distinction, less the wisdom. Silver at the temples, sparse on top and one tweed jacket away from looking like I lecture here.

Then I spent three months at the council, checking whether any of it worked outside a classroom. It did, which surprised nobody more than me.

Now for my second act. In the time I spent studying AI, AI rearranged the job market. I think it won the first round.

Still here, still conscious? Congrats, you've made it to the small print.

My research contract ends in November. I'm not a data scientist. I'm a Head of Marketing who can translate between the technical and the commercial and embed AI in how a team actually works.

If you're hiring, know someone who is, or just fancy a coffee and a chat, my inbox is open. Right now, it's less Amazon, more Mojave, so talk to me, or there's a sequel coming, and it's longer.

Done a mid-career reset yourself? I'd be interested in what changed on the other side. And did the new skills get you hired, or just get you in the room? If the answer involves 60p VRBs, I have follow-up questions.

If you've been job hunting in privacy or compliance recently, you've probably seen the posting.

One role. One headcount. And a requirements list that reads like three or four separate job descriptions stitched together: GDPR, privacy operations, AI governance, information security, SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIST, vendor risk management, incident response, and sometimes even contract review and legal advisory thrown in for good measure.

That's not one job. That's an entire department disguised as a single hire.

I understand why this happens. A company that's only now building this function often doesn't know how to break it down, because no one internally has done this work before. So the job posting becomes a wish list instead of a role definition. Leadership knows they need "someone who handles all the compliance stuff," and that's exactly how it ends up written.

But the result is a hire who's set up to struggle from day one. No single person can be simultaneously deep in data protection law, fluent in ISO 27001 audit mechanics, running a DSR pipeline, building an AI governance framework, and managing vendor risk assessments, all at a senior level, alone.

What tends to actually happen after that hire starts:

▪️They triage. Whatever creates the most immediate risk or regulatory pressure gets attention, everything else waits

▪️Something eventually breaks, usually the thing that got deprioritized, and it looks like the hire underperformed rather than the role being impossible

▪️Or the company realizes within a year that it actually needs three or four people, not one, and starts hiring around the original hire

If you're the one hiring, the fix is deciding what actually needs to happen in the first six months, and building the role around that, not around every framework the company might eventually need.

If you're the one being hired, it's worth asking directly in the interview: which of these areas am I expected to own versus just be aware of. The answer tells you a lot about whether the company understands what it's asking for.

Have you come across this pattern in your own job search or hiring process?
